questions.stem: What does 'like dissolves like' pair together?

options.text: Solutes and solvents with matching intermolecular force types
options.explanation: Matching forces let new solute-solvent attractions replace the old ones.
The principle spans all phase combinations.
Ionic solutes need polar, ion-surrounding solvents.
That is exactly the mismatch the principle rejects.

questions.stem: Why does ethanol mix with water in all proportions?

options.explanation: Both carry polar O-H groups.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds form between ethanol's O-H hydrogen and water's oxygens
options.explanation: The shared force type makes the pair interchangeable.
The hydrocarbon part is the insoluble end, not the mixer.
No ionisation occurs on mixing.

questions.stem: Why does hexanol dissolve poorly in water compared with ethanol?

options.explanation: Ethanol proves the opposite.
It remains a covalent molecular liquid.

options.text: Its long non-polar chain dilutes the one hydrogen-bonding site
options.explanation: The polar fraction shrinks as the chain grows.

options.text: Its OH group stops hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: The hydroxyl still works; the chain outvotes it.

questions.stem: Why do giant covalent substances resist dissolving in every solvent?

options.text: They are too light to sink into a solvent
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant to solubility here.
No universal repulsion exists.

options.text: They hydrogen bond to themselves too strongly
options.explanation: Giant covalent networks have no molecular hydrogen bonding.

options.text: Overcoming their covalent lattice bonds costs more energy than any solvent supplies
options.explanation: The network's bond energy prices it out of solution.

questions.stem: A polar covalent solute lands in a non-polar solvent. What happens?

options.text: Its dipole-dipole attractions cannot interact well with the solvent, so it barely dissolves
options.explanation: The mismatch strands the solute.
That is the like-likes outcome, not this one.
Ionisation requires chemical reaction, not mixing.

options.text: It becomes non-polar to fit in
options.explanation: Molecules do not restructure to suit solvents.

questions.stem: State the general principle governing solvent choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Like dissolves like: non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents and polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, through matching force types.

questions.stem: Quote the alcohol pair that demonstrates the chain-length effect on solubility.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol, C2H5OH, is readily soluble in water while hexanol, C6H13OH, is not.

questions.stem: Explain why solubility of covalent molecules can decrease as they become larger.
questions.modelAnswer: The polar part of the molecule is a fixed fraction of its surface; as the molecule grows, that fraction shrinks relative to the non-polar bulk, so solvent contacts the polar site less often and dissolution pays worse.

questions.stem: A series of alcohols adds CH2 per step, each step swelling the non-polar fraction by about 14 mass units against a fixed 17-unit OH group. Estimate the non-polar share for hexanol, C6H13OH, to the nearest whole percent.
questions.modelAnswer: The chain carries 85 of 102 mass units, about 83 percent, leaving the tiny polar share that strands hexanol from water.

questions.stem: Why are haloalkanes only partially soluble in water?

options.explanation: The C-X bond is polar covalent, not ionic.

options.text: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
options.explanation: No bond in a haloalkane joins hydrogen to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen.
The C-X bond is polar; the hydrogen-bond capacity is what fails.
Alcohols dissolve readily.

questions.stem: Which feature would make a haloalkane more water-soluble?

options.explanation: Longer chains worsen water solubility.
Polarity helps, not hurts.

options.text: Adding a hydroxyl group to the molecule
options.explanation: An O-H bond restores hydrogen-bond capacity, as in halogenated alcohols.

options.text: Replacing chlorine with a heavier halogen
options.explanation: Heavier halogens swell the non-polar fraction.

questions.stem: Which ends of water molecules surround a dissolved cation?

options.explanation: Like charges repel; that orientation cannot hold.
Ions contact lone-pair or dipole regions, not bond axes.
Hydration is oriented, not random.
The negative pole faces the positive ion.

questions.stem: Why is calcium chloride less soluble in water than sodium chloride?

options.text: The 2+ cation's lattice attractions are stronger, and higher charge generally lowers solubility
options.explanation: Doubly charged ions hold the lattice harder.
It is an ionic compound.

options.text: Chloride ions are bigger in that salt
options.explanation: The anion is identical in both.
NaCl has no hydrogen at all.

questions.stem: What two factors does the solubility of an ionic compound depend on?

options.explanation: The mechanism factors are lattice disruption and hydration.

options.text: Breaking down the ionic lattice and the surrounding of ions by polar molecules
options.explanation: Both costs and payoffs enter the balance.

options.text: Melting point and boiling point of the solute
options.explanation: Those are bulk properties, not the dissolution mechanism.

options.text: The colour and odour of the ions
options.explanation: Neither affects solubility.

questions.stem: State what water does to an ionic lattice when a compound dissolves.
questions.modelAnswer: Water disrupts the ionic lattice and surrounds each ion, with delta-positive hydrogens facing the anion and delta-negative oxygens facing the cation.

questions.stem: Quote the solubility figures for sodium chloride and calcium chloride in one dm3 of water.
questions.modelAnswer: About 356.9 g of sodium chloride dissolves per dm3 of water; calcium chloride manages only 74.4 g in that same volume.

questions.stem: Explain why polarity alone does not make a compound water-soluble.
questions.modelAnswer: Water's network is built of hydrogen bonds, so a compound joins it only by forming hydrogen bonds itself; a polar bond without a donor hydrogen, as in haloalkanes, offers nothing to that network and solubility stays partial.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride dissolves 356.9 g per dm3 while calcium chloride manages 74.4 g. How many times more soluble, to one decimal place, is the sodium salt by these figures?
questions.modelAnswer: Dividing 356.9 by 74.4 gives about 4.8, the solubility ratio that the charge penalty buys.
